Kautukabera
(‘image with thread’)
------------------------------------------
Hindu temples have two types of images: the one fixed permanently in the गर्भगृह or sanctum sanctorum called ‘dhruvabera’ and the one kept separately in a room or a shed, which is used during the processions on special days. This processional image is normally a smaller replica of the original image, made of pañcaloha or bronze and is called ‘utsava-mūrti’.
‘Kautuka’ is the technical name for a sacred thread that is wound round the right wrist of the उत्सवमूर्ति on the night prior to the रथोत्सव or procession-festival. Hence, this उत्सवमूर्ति is also called ‘Kautukabera’.
See also UTSAVAMŪRTI.

Kautsasūkta
------------------------------------------
Sins and their expiation is one of the important subjects dealt with in the smṛtis and धर्मशास्त्रस्. Apart from paścāttāpa (regretting for having committed the sins) which is a prerequisite, many modes are described for getting rid of or for lessening the effects of sins. One such is जप or the muttering of some Vedic mantras.
The Manusmṛti (11.249) mentions that by the जप of the Kautsa (sūkta) even a drinker of surā or wine becomes pure.
The eight mantras of Ṛgveda (1.97.1-8) attributed to the sage Kautsa are known as the Kautsasūkta. The sage Kautsa is said to have prayed to अग्नि (the god of fire) for freeing him from the sin of killing a woman.
He had killed a demoness called Dīrghajihvī at the instance of इन्द्र, since she was troubling the sages engaged in the performance of sacrifices.
All the eight ṛks of this सूक्त end with the words ap naḥ śośucadagham, ‘May our sin depart from us!’
